findings.title: The buffer empties the batch array before the delayed write reads it, so every audit batch is lost
findings.scenario: With auditBatchSize=2, two archive requests call recordAudit. EventBuffer.flush calls writer.write(this.items), which only schedules `events.map(toLine)` inside `.then(...)`. flush then runs `this.items.length = 0` right away, on the same array. findings.title: A failed audit write is now only logged, and shutdown still reports success
findings.scenario: Make the audit file unwritable (EACCES, or the disk is full). Before, appendFileSync threw and the failure reached the caller. findings.whyNotPrevented: onError defaults to console.error. Nothing retries the write, rethrows the error, or tracks failures for idle() to report. No test covers a failed write.

findings.scenario: Range 2026-01-01 to 2026-01-03, with a renewal recorded at 2026-01-02T00:00:00Z. chargeRenewal always records at startOfDay. The renewal is counted in the 2026-01-01 row (its upper bound is inclusive) and again in the 2026-01-02 row. The range totalCents is then too high by the renewal price. findings.title: Plan inheritance now depends on the order of the switch cases

findings.scenario: Today the code works: enterprise returns all six features, team four, free two. The risk is a later edit. If someone adds a new case (say 'pro') between 'team' and 'free', or reorders the cases, plans silently gain or lose features. Before, FREE_FEATURES and TEAM_FEATURES built each plan explicitly. Adding `const ENTERPRISE_FEATURES = [...TEAM_FEATURES, 'sso', 'audit-log']` and a `case 'enterprise': return [...ENTERPRISE_FEATURES];` would have kept that pattern. The rewrite also leans on the '// falls through' comment to get past the project's 'no-fallthrough': 'error' lint rule.

findings.title: Plan inheritance now depends on the order of the switch cases
findings.scenario: The old code built each plan from the one below it (TEAM_FEATURES = [...FREE_FEATURES, ...]). findings.scenario: The provider sends a signed in_transit event for a shipmentId that is not in the shipments Map (for example, after a process restart clears the in-memory Map). updateShipment returns null, but the handler still replies 200 { ok: true }. findings.title: Writes saved values into the shared DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object, so one user's preferences show up for other users
findings.scenario: User A has savedPreferences {theme:'dark'} and user B has none. Calling getUser(A) changes DEFAULT_PREFERENCES.theme to 'dark' for good. A later getUser(B) then returns theme 'dark' instead of 'light', so one user's settings show up for another. The defaults stay changed for the rest of the process.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaultPreferences() in src/defaults.js:8 returns the same DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object on every call, not a copy. Nothing freezes or clones it, and the repo has no tests.

findings.title: The `in` check accepts inherited keys like __proto__, toString and constructor as supported preferences
findings.scenario: Stored preferences_json is '{"toString":1,"__proto__":{"x":1}}'. JSON.parse makes both own keys, so Object.entries returns them. `'toString' in preferences` is true because the key is inherited, so the value is copied in. Assigning preferences['__proto__'] replaces the object's prototype. The response then carries keys the app no longer supports, or has a changed prototype, which is the opposite of the intent to ignore those keys.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` looks up the prototype chain, nothing else checks that the key is an own key, and the repo has no tests.

findings.whyNotPrevented: The repo has no test files.

findings.scenario: User A has savedPreferences {theme:'dark'}. GET /users/A returns theme 'dark'. Then GET /users/B, who has no saved preferences, also returns theme 'dark', because defaultPreferences() returned the same module-level object that A's request changed. Every request after that sees the changed defaults.

findings.title: The `in` check looks at the prototype chain, so inherited names like `__proto__` and `constructor` get through as supported keys
findings.scenario: A stored preferences_json of '{"__proto__":{"admin":true},"constructor":1}' is JSON.parsed into own keys `__proto__` and `constructor`. `'__proto__' in preferences` is true, so the assignment replaces the object's prototype and the response picks up inherited fields. `constructor` is kept as an extra key. Either way, keys we no longer support are not ignored.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No check for own properties (Object.hasOwn) and no allowlist of the default keys. Nothing validates savedPreferences when it is saved or loaded.

findings.title: The `in` check also accepts inherited keys like toString and __proto__, so unsupported keys get through
findings.scenario: A stored preferences_json of {"toString":"x"} or {"constructor":1} passes `key in preferences` through the prototype chain and appears in the response. findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` walks the prototype chain. Object.hasOwn would not. The stored JSON is user-supplied data saved by saveUser and is not validated.
